title: Land Is Not a Commodity: Why a Land Value Tax Can Cure the Housing Crisis
dek: The housing shortage is only a symptom; the real disease is land monopoly. A land value tax shifts the burden from buildings to land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, and returning location value to society instead of fattening landlords.
why: The land value tax is an overlooked lever that economists across the left and right agree on. Lars Doucet uses Houston parking lots, South Korea's appraisal system, and Norway's resource dividend to turn an abstract tax regime into a power struggle.
who: Economists concerned with housing policy, urban planners, real estate developers, and investors and policy researchers who want to know whether the "land tax" is worth betting on.

points.h: A land tax is not a property tax, it is a location tax
points.body: Lars builds his case with an analogy: the land value tax and the ordinary property tax share the same origin, but the LVT separates "building value" from "land value." A building tax punishes you for constructing, maintaining, and renovating; a land tax only punishes you for occupying a good location and letting it sit idle. He says land value comes from the labor of those around you—your ability to earn a living, go to school, and make friends the moment you step outside depends entirely on your neighbors and the whole city. The landlord lies back and sucks this collective value into his own pocket. This is the paradox of Progress and Poverty: ballpoint pens fell from $270 to 11 cents, but land never does.

points.h: The YIMBYs are right, but not right enough
points.body: The host asks: Oakland relaxed density and rents fell, so do we still need a land tax? Lars concedes that the "housing shortage" is the main cause, but points out that YIMBYs fail to explain a counterexample: Houston has no zoning, yet its downtown still has a giant surface parking lot worth $500 million. Why? Because the property tax bundles land and building together, so the more you build the more tax you pay, while holding out for appreciation is cheaper. Developers therefore have no incentive to develop, only an incentive to lobby for rezoning and then keep holding. He says reform without a land tax leads to a stalemate: "You changed the zoning, but I just won't sell."

points.h: The objections are built on imagination
points.body: Lars groups the opposition into three categories and dismantles each. How do you appraise land separately from buildings? He says 14,000 appraisal jurisdictions worldwide already do something similar; South Korea manually reviews 500,000 sample parcels a year and produces nationwide land values in 5 months; Norway trained a national automated valuation model on the state property data platform Finn.no with a core team of just 3 people. Think there will be too many protests? He says the real source of protest is "the land looks the same as next door, why charge me more"—under a land tax, you and your neighbor are assessed on the same location basis, which actually makes it easier. The excuse for not doing it is that no one has measured it.

points.h: The little old lady is not a reason to object
points.body: The sharpest criticism is "transitional unfairness"—the day a land tax is announced, existing landowners instantly bear the capitalized burden of all future taxes, amounting to a one-time expropriation. Lars acknowledges this is a Gordon Tullock-style transition trap, then offers safeguards: the action is never a one-step nationwide 100% land tax, but a gradual switch by school district or county; run revenue-neutral simulations, and most single-family homes actually see their tax bills fall. As for the elderly afraid of being driven from their old homes, he says Texas already has a tax deferral system: owe now, and after death the estate pays it back with interest.

points.h: Britain's failure was a capacity problem
points.body: The most commonly cited counterexample online is Britain's 1910s "People's Budget": the valuation took 6 years and was overturned by shopkeepers' protests and the courts. Lars's response is blunt: that widely shared article is simply "deriving a universal law from one sample," and it simultaneously claims that "a pure land tax has never succeeded" and that "land cannot be valued"—yet South Korea has been appraising nationwide land values parcel by parcel for decades. He says this only proves that the British state apparatus was weak, not that a land tax is theoretically unworkable. His tone hardens: if you want to be a serious critic, you have to go find counterexamples, not pass off lazy ignorance as a verdict.

points.h: Norway achieved Georgism through a resource dividend
points.body: Lars points to a fact that makes Norway a "success story" today: Norway's entire national resource management regime is Georgist in structure—natural resources like oil are recognized as the property of all the people, and extractors pay extremely high resource taxes, but production and investment themselves are not punished, so entrepreneurship is encouraged while the natural dividend is captured for the treasury and used to fund universal welfare. Norway's Georgism is almost perfect, except it is not on land value tax. This "Norwegian paradox" leads him to assert: the land tax is not the enemy of the welfare state; it can be its foundation.

points.h: The automobile opened a second frontier
points.body: Lars explains why the land question that was hotly debated everywhere a century ago later disappeared: the frontier itself is a mechanism of "free land"—as long as you can expand into the wilderness, the lower classes don't have to face the squeeze of "high work + high rent." America's first frontier was westward expansion; when it closed, Henry George appeared. In the 20th century the automobile turned the suburbs into a "second frontier," extending it for another 80 years, until it closed again around 2006-2008. He says people now call it a "second Gilded Age," but it is just the script from over a hundred years ago with a new cast, and post-pandemic remote work as a "third frontier" lasted only about 5 minutes before capital digested it.

points.h: Don't win online, do the politicians' homework
points.body: The closing answer to the last question is very practical: Lars says the most effective way to create change he has learned in the past 5 years is not arguing with keyboard warriors, but taking every objection a state senator or city council member might raise, preparing data simulations and ready answers in advance, and putting them directly on their desks—he calls "doing politicians' homework" an absurd but extraordinarily effective strategy. Today several states have already passed bills allowing land value tax reform. His call to action: go measure, don't guess.

terms.def: An annual tax levied on the value of land rather than the total value of real estate, which does not punish building improvements.
The 19th-century idea launched by Henry George: land is common wealth, and land rent should be captured by society.
A movement advocating loosening land-use zoning regulations and allowing more housing to be built.
Using a unified model and sample parcels to automatically value properties across an entire jurisdiction, rather than assessing each one on site.
The Georgist ideal: tax only land value and abolish all other taxes on labor and capital.
The high rents extracted from natural resources (such as oil), captured for all citizens.
